There's a few things I think about this. 1) Technology is better. 2) Tastes (or what companies target) have changed.

Point 1: Technology has made making a pretty anime much easier and cheaper compared to 'the early days', making cost less of a barrier to entry and allowing higher quantity of anime to be made. What is the 'technology' I'm talking about? Things like computer assisted drawing, coloring for individual animation cels, and some more examples Production IG thought up. 3D animation, which has been used more recently, also has a tendency to be cheaper than 2D animation since it only requires a 3D model be made and animated instead of having cels redrawn frame by frame. These technologies reduce time required to complete a task or animation effect, and in turn reduce cost. With average anime being easier to create, more people try to make some and higher quantity of anime is being created than before. This of course, does not mean the amount of quality talent scales up with the inflated amount of anime, so there are still amazing anime around but they're competing with higher quantity of anime.

Point 2: Anime used to have a reputation for being mostly for sci-fi, and companies that sponsored anime (so they had money to happen) were usually toy companies that could make their money back by selling toys (think Transformers). This has only changed nowadays in the sense that it's not specifically toys that are being sold, but the potential to merchandise and sell discs. Of course anime that are commercially successful tend to go on forever and ever because the merch nets consistent profits. Instead of sci-fi and mechas now though, we have more moe and the Big Three. So that kind of pandering hasn't gone away, it's just changed face. Also, for adaptations, the anime are partially created to increase sales in the source material and increase exposure.

TL;DR...

  1. Technology has made anime easier to produce, thereby changing the quantity we see, but the amount of unique talent does not scale up wih the anime quantity.

  2. The rise of moe is merely a replacement of old anime's large amount of sci-fi and mecha, with both being each era's perceived 'ultimate otaku pandering' and best chance to make money without as much original idea and unique talent needed.

Anime's best hits now are not worse than any other era's, it's just harder to filter out the bad anime to get to the 'good stuff'.

Anime, I think, isn't necessarily getting worse, just a lot more visible. Anime was, and still is, a very niche medium in the West; for all its gains in popularity over the past decade it's easy to forget that it was even more obscure in the early 00s, 90s, and 80s.

The fact of the matter is that two things conspired to make "older" anime whitewashed for quality:

  1. Bad anime didn't get exported. Bebop, Evangelion, Dragonball - these were hugely popular shows that were commercially successful enough to get a release in the West. There were dozens of shitty shows that were never given exposure and were therefore forgotten!
  2. People don't remember bland shows. You remember good shows because you like them, rewatch them, and refer people to them; you remember bad shows because you use them as example of what not to do; but bland, average shows don't stick in the memory. Anybody remember, I dunno, Nogizaka Haruka? Generic romcom from summer 2008. Heard of it? Seen it? Probably not - it was average. People don't bring it up as an example of good storytelling or terrible mistakes because it was average. And there's a lot of average stuff every season!

So, on top of two factors (economic and psychological) conspiring to make it so that we only remember the best and worst of older generations of anime, we also have to look at the fact that anime is more accessible now than ever before. As I just mentioned, it used to be that only good, 100%-surefire anime got exported, which meant that by default almost anything that got to the West was bound to be good. Nowadays, though, we have a very prolific fansub network (thanks, internet!) as well as a rapidly expanding streaming industry (Crunchy, Funi, Animelab, Hulu, Netflix even!). And this isn't just anime - light novels, visual novels, manga are all being exported to the West in greater numbers than ever before. The problem is that as you increase volume, you inherently lose quality control.

It's like the situation with Steam Greenlight - making access to a medium easier for the consumer means it's easier for the producers to get more shit through the filter. Shows that wouldn't have stood a chance in a Western market commercially - the otaku-pandering harem shows, the shity adaptations, and so on - now get exposure by warrant of the anime market being easier to get into. Furthermore, because of the volume of anime we now have access to, we get saturated more easily. When you only have access to two shows a season, it's hard to get to the point where you think "Man, there's just too much mecha nowadays." When you have access to dozens of shows a season, four of which are mecha, then that situation changes!

tl;dr: Sturgeon's Law.

Sturgeon's Law says "90% of everything is shit." This is true for any and all types of media (the corollary is "if less than 90% of something is shit, your standards are too low"), anime included. Back in the day, it used to be that, due to a variety of factors, we only saw the 10% and saw very little of the 90% - we didn't see the shit, and even then we had such a small frame of reference that we didn't see shit for what it was. Nowadays, having access to everything and having higher personal standards, it appears as if the industry has gone from "100% quality to 90% shit" when in reality it's just we're seeing it as it is for the first time.

Alternatively, to answer the original question more directly, I'd say that anime has generally gotten better over the years, on average. This is primarily thanks to economy of scale - just like gaming, an influx of technologies and abundant talent has raised the floor on quality standards. What is nowadays considered "shit animation" would've been considered god-tier years ago; likewise for the current state of voice acting (for both Japanese and English seiyuu). Seriously, dubs used to be absolutely unwatchable to the point that even non-fans would recognize it was shit, nowadays even the worst Sentai dub cast can pull off a tolerable performance.

Of course, lowering the floor does not equally raise the ceiling, which contributes to the problem - we expect "great" to be something that's significantly better than everything else, but you run into the problem of diminishing returns. Even though modern tech and talent pools can make a shitty anime average, the same tools and talent won't make a good anime a masterpiece because the amount of work and luck required is orders of magnitude greater.

I find it an interesting topic, but very subjective depending on who you ask. For me, the quality hasn't dropped. I still think the anime I grew up are part of the pinnacle. It's what got me interested in the first place. I think it was similarly described as, looking through rose color glasses. When you first start watching anime, it's a whole new world. Full of new things and it's exciting. Eventually, those anime that got you in, become the classics, the nostalgia, with many other shows simply fading into obscurity.

I do think the higher quantity of anime makes it easier to notice an increased number of bad anime, but at the same time, it creates more competition. The average anime fan only has so much time to watch any one anime during a given season. So with the larger number of anime, the higher the expectation. You want a show to be great, because by watching said show, you're missing out on a dozen others.

In the end though, I think it's simply the fact that anime, like all forms of entertainment, is simply changing, constantly. Moe may be popular now, but give it a few years and it'll move onto the next new thing. If the only reason you liked anime is because 80% of it was mecha and sci-fi, then the change will likely lead to you losing interest. I do think anime has gotten 'better', as in the level of quality afforded to highly anticipated titles (think Fate) has definitely put anime to a new level. However the extra quantity will leave a bad taste since it's hard to tell what anime will have quality.

On a side note, I do find it unfortunate that the higher number of anime is leading to several shows to be less viewed. They don't necessarily have to be great, but plenty of decent shows will be overshadowed or forgotten pretty quickly. A quick example for me would be Donten Ni Wauru. I loved that show personally, and it was received pretty well by others who watched it, yet completely forgotten despite only being *last year. *
